title: Playdough
strapline: Squeezing, rolling and pinching — strong little hands building big ideas.
intent: Build hand and finger strength through squeezing, pinching, rolling and pressing — the groundwork for later pencil control.
Learn how a material changes and responds: dough stretches, squashes, springs back, dries out, softens with warm hands.
Use tools with purpose — rollers, cutters, scissors, garlic presses — choosing the right one for the job.
Explore early maths through dividing, sharing, comparing sizes and counting out pieces, candles and balls.
Represent ideas in a material that forgives every mistake — a cake can become a snake and back again in seconds.
Talk while making: narrating, describing textures and negotiating over tools and dough.
implementation: Make the dough with the children, not for them — measuring flour, salt and water is half the learning, and they see a recipe become a material.
Sit and play alongside, modelling techniques without taking over: roll a sausage, pinch a hedgehog spike, flatten a pancake, and let them borrow what's useful.
Feed in precise vocabulary as hands work: squash, stretch, twist, coil, flatten, crumbly, smooth, springy.
Offer dough scissors and snipping challenges for children building scissor skills — dough gives more resistance and more success than paper.
Add weight to the work sometimes — a big, stiff batch for two-handed kneading and whole-arm effort, a soft batch for fine finger work.
Resist the cutter takeover: keep days where it's just dough, hands and boards, so children invent rather than stamp.
Notice and name effort out loud — 'you kept rolling until it was long enough' matters more than 'lovely snake'.
key_questions: What is your dough turning into?
What happens if you squash it flat — can you get it back?
Which tool do you think will make that shape?
How could you make one big enough for everyone?
Whose ball is bigger — how do you know?
What does it feel like in your hands today?

impact.text: Younger children squeeze, poke and pull the dough with whole-hand and fist movements, enjoying the material for its own sake.
Children snip dough with scissors, with the grip moving from fist towards fingers.
Children choose rollers, cutters and presses with intent, and older children work with real precision and patience — a candle in each corner, a face with tiny features.
Children narrate and direct as they make — 'this is the birthday cake, you be the mummy' — using talk to carry the play.
Children pick up and try out the making words the adult feeds in — coil, flatten, springy — in their own talk.
Children set out to make something particular — 'I'm making a hedgehog' — and adapt when the spikes flop.
Children compare their sausages and balls — longer, fatter, biggest — and divide the dough so everyone gets some.
Children count out candles, balls and pieces accurately, knowing the last number tells them how many.

enhancements: Herb bundles and scissors — rosemary and mint to snip and knead in, changing the smell and the talk.
Birthday-candle counting — a tub of candles and number cards next to plain dough cakes.
A stiff, cold batch straight from the fridge next to a warm soft one — same recipe, different material.
Loose parts tray: buttons, pasta shapes, matchsticks, googly eyes — for faces, patterns and hedgehogs.
Real baking follow-up: use the same rolling and cutting skills on real biscuit dough in the kitchen.
A 'dough gym' five minutes — squeeze, roll, pinch, poke to music — before children who need it settle to fine work.
Recipe cards with pictures so children can lead the next batch themselves.

playing_exploring: Children get stuck in with hands first, finding out what the dough will and won't do.
They use familiar dough in new pretend ways — cakes, snails, dinner for the baby.
active_learning: Kneading a stiff batch or rolling a snake 'long enough' takes real persistence, and children feel the win.
They keep adjusting — more squashing, another roll — until it looks like the thing in their head.
creating_thinking: One lump becomes many things in a session; children test their own ideas cheaply because nothing is ever ruined.
They plan, change the plan, and find their own ways round a floppy spike or a cracked pancake.
